original_question: Describe the dynamics of generic trajectories in parallelogram tiling billiards, where the plane is tiled by parallelograms with side vectors a_vec = (a, 0) and b_vec = (b sin alpha, b cos alpha) and the dynamics depends on the parameters alpha in (0, pi) and m = a/b.
target_in_paper: Olga Paris-Romaskevich, "Tiling billiards," Question 2, with nearby context from Proposition 3. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.12896))
correct_elements: Your draft already matches the paper's exact target very closely: it identifies the correct model (parallelogram tiling billiards), the paper's parametrization by a_vec=(a,0) and b_vec=(b sin alpha, b cos alpha), the angle range alpha in (0,pi), the scale-free parameter m=a/b, and the focus on generic trajectory dynamics. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.12896))
missing_details: The paper's definition of a tiling billiard should be made explicit: trajectories move in straight lines inside tiles and, when crossing an edge, their direction changes by Snell's law of refraction with coefficient -1; this is not ordinary reflective billiards. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.12896))
The underlying tiling is a periodic tiling of R^2 by copies of a single parallelogram whose sides are parallel to a_vec and b_vec. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.12896))
The positivity assumptions a,b>0 are part of the paper's setup (written there as a,b in R_+^*). ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.12896))

The official wording is 'describe the dynamics of (at least, generic) trajectories,' so a fully faithful restatement should preserve that quantifier rather than speak only about generic trajectories. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.12896))

A stand-alone version should implicitly restrict to nonsingular trajectories / generic initial conditions avoiding vertices, since the nearby discussion passes to the plane with vertices removed when formulating the foldability analysis. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.12896))

Nearby context matters: the paper presents parallelogram tiling billiards as one of the simplest non-locally-foldable periodic tilings on which to test the broader classification of generic behaviors, contrasting them with locally foldable periodic tiling billiards, which are integrable under technical regularity assumptions. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.12896))

Proposition 3 gives the main nearby sharpening: the universal cover is foldable exactly when alpha is one of {pi/12, 5pi/12, pi/6, pi/3, pi/8, 3pi/8, pi/4} and Q a_vec + Q b_vec is invariant under rotation by 4 alpha; the paper notes that alpha=pi/4 is the simplest case. This is not an equivalent reformulation of the question, but it is the paper's main special regime for attack. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.12896))
refined_question: For the tiling billiard on the periodic tiling of R^2 by copies of a single parallelogram, where a particle moves linearly inside each tile and, upon crossing an edge, is refracted according to Snell's law with refraction coefficient -1, and where the tile has sides parallel to a_vec=(a,0) and b_vec=(b sin alpha, b cos alpha) with a,b>0, alpha in (0,pi), and shape parameter m=a/b, describe the dynamics of the trajectories, at least for generic initial conditions, as a function of the parameters (alpha,m). ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.12896))
justification: The draft is essentially a near-verbatim restatement of Question 2 in the Olga Paris-Romaskevich contribution, so the correct target is that question itself, not the broader neighboring Question 1 about all periodic tiling billiards. The rewrite only restores the paper's hidden assumptions and model definition: refraction coefficient -1, periodic tiling by one parallelogram, a,b>0, and the exact quantifier 'at least, generic.' Proposition 3 is nearby auxiliary context rather than an equivalent reformulation: it identifies the special parameter regime where the universal cover is foldable and may reduce the study to dynamics on translation surfaces, with alpha=pi/4 singled out as the simplest case. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.12896))
